people/miguel-de-molinos/summary: Spanish priest in Rome whose Spiritual Guide (1675) taught a passive prayer of quiet and total abandonment to God. Arrested in 1685, he was condemned for "quietism" by Innocent XI’s bull Coelestis Pastor (1687) and died in prison.
people/madame-guyon/summary: French widow and mystic whose Short and Easy Method of Prayer (1685) taught simple abandonment and pure love. Imprisoned in the Bastille, she was at the centre of the quietist controversy between Bossuet and Fénelon; her writings were later beloved by Pietists, Quakers and Holiness Protestants.
people/madame-guyon/keyIdeas/0: Prayer of the heart for all
people/thomas-merton/summary: Trappist monk of Gethsemani Abbey, Kentucky, whose autobiography The Seven Storey Mountain (1948) and New Seeds of Contemplation (1961) popularised contemplative prayer for modern readers. He engaged in dialogue with Buddhists and wrote on peace and race; he died in Bangkok in 1968 during an interreligious monastic meeting.
people/thomas-merton/keyIdeas/0: Contemplation as awareness of God’s presence
people/thomas-keating/summary: Abbot of St Joseph’s Abbey, Spencer, Massachusetts, who with William Meninger and Basil Pennington developed Centering Prayer in the 1970s from The Cloud of Unknowing, and founded Contemplative Outreach (1984) to teach it widely.
people/thomas-keating/keyIdeas/1: Consent to God’s presence and action
people/diodore-of-tarsus/summary: Teacher of an ascetic school (asketerion) at Antioch and bishop of Tarsus from 378. He taught John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia and became the father of the Antiochene method of exegesis, which favoured the historical sense of Scripture and a disciplined "theoria" over free allegory. His works survive mostly in fragments after posthumous condemnation of his Christology.
people/peter-lombard/summary: Italian-born master of the cathedral school of Paris and briefly its bishop (1159-60). His Four Books of Sentences (c.1155-58) arranged patristic opinions, above all Augustine’s, by topic and harmonised apparent conflicts; it became the standard theology textbook of the medieval universities, on which every master had to comment.
people/peter-lombard/keyIdeas/2: The Holy Spirit as the charity in believers
people/gabriel-biel/summary: German priest, Brother of the Common Life and first professor of theology at Tübingen, often called the last of the scholastics. His Collectorium on Lombard’s Sentences systematised the via moderna of Ockham; his teaching that God gives grace to those who "do what is in them" was the theology Luther studied and later attacked.
people/gabriel-biel/keyIdeas/2: Absolute and ordained power of God
people/lorenzo-valla/summary: Italian humanist whose philological critique exposed the Donation of Constantine as a forgery (1440) and whose Annotations on the New Testament compared the Vulgate with the Greek. Erasmus published the Annotations in 1505, carrying the humanist call to the sources into biblical scholarship.
people/lorenzo-valla/keyIdeas/0: Philology as a tool of theology
people/lorenzo-valla/keyIdeas/1: Critique of the Donation of Constantine
people/lorenzo-valla/keyIdeas/2: Return to the Greek New Testament
people/francis-turretin/summary: Geneva-born Reformed pastor and professor whose Institutes of Elenctic Theology (1679-85) is the most influential compendium of Reformed orthodoxy. Using scholastic question-and-answer method, it defended Reformed doctrine against Catholic, Socinian, Lutheran and Remonstrant views, and was the main textbook at Princeton until the late 19th century.
people/johann-gerhard/summary: Professor at Jena and the most important theologian of Lutheran orthodoxy. His Loci theologici (1610-22) gave Lutheran doctrine a full scholastic form, while his Sacred Meditations (1606) show the devotional warmth that coexisted with orthodox method.
people/august-hermann-francke/summary: Leading organiser of German Pietism after a conversion experience in 1687. At Halle he founded an orphanage, schools, a Bible institute and a printing house (the Franckesche Stiftungen), trained theologians to value conversion and practical piety, and sent the first Protestant missionaries to India (Tranquebar, 1706).
people/william-perkins/summary: Cambridge preacher and the most widely read English Puritan theologian of his generation. A Golden Chaine (1590) set out Reformed predestination as the chain of salvation, while his casuistry and treatises on assurance and preaching shaped the "practical divinity" of Puritan pastors in England, New England and the Netherlands.
people/william-perkins/keyIdeas/0: Theology as the science of living blessedly
people/william-perkins/keyIdeas/1: Practical divinity and cases of conscience
people/john-toland/summary: Irish-born freethinker whose Christianity not Mysterious (1696) argued that nothing in the Gospel is contrary to reason or above it. The book was condemned by the Irish Parliament and became a founding text of English Deism.
people/john-toland/keyIdeas/0: Reason as the test of revelation
people/immanuel-kant/summary: Königsberg philosopher raised in Pietism whose Critique of Pure Reason (1781) denied that speculative reason can prove God, freedom or immortality, while Religion within the Bounds of Mere Reason (1793) reinterpreted Christianity as moral religion. Every later Protestant theology had to answer him.
people/albrecht-ritschl/summary: Göttingen theologian whose Christian Doctrine of Justification and Reconciliation (1870-74) grounded faith in the historical Jesus and the ethical Kingdom of God, rejecting metaphysics and mysticism. His school (Harnack, Herrmann) dominated German Protestantism before 1914 and fed the social gospel.
people/albrecht-ritschl/keyIdeas/1: Kingdom of God as ethical community
people/paul-tillich/summary: German Lutheran theologian, dismissed by the Nazis in 1933, who taught at Union, Harvard and Chicago. His Systematic Theology (1951-63) used a "method of correlation" in which existential questions raised by human finitude are answered by the symbols of revelation, and spoke of God as the ground of being and the object of ultimate concern.
people/georges-florovsky/summary: Russian émigré Orthodox priest and patristic scholar (Paris, then Harvard and Princeton). At the Athens congress of 1936 he called for a "neo-patristic synthesis" freeing Orthodox theology from its "Western captivity"; his Ways of Russian Theology (1937) sharply criticised Russian religious philosophy. A founding figure of the World Council of Churches.
people/georges-florovsky/keyIdeas/1: Acquiring the mind of the Fathers
people/vladimir-lossky/summary: Russian Orthodox lay theologian in Paris whose Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church (1944) presented apophaticism, the Palamite essence-energies distinction and deification as the heart of Orthodoxy, and made the filioque central to East-West difference.
people/dumitru-staniloae/summary: Romanian Orthodox priest-theologian, imprisoned by the communist regime 1958-63, who translated the Philokalia into Romanian (from 1946) and wrote a three-volume Orthodox Dogmatic Theology (1978), combining neo-patristic theology with personalism.
people/dumitru-staniloae/keyIdeas/1: World as gift and dialogue of love
people/henri-de-lubac/summary: French Jesuit, wounded in the First World War and active in the spiritual resistance to Nazism, whose Catholicism (1938) and Surnaturel (1946) recovered the Fathers’ vision of the social and spiritual character of the faith and challenged the neo-scholastic idea of "pure nature". Silenced in the 1950s, he was a peritus at Vatican II and made a cardinal in 1983.
people/yves-congar/summary: French Dominican ecclesiologist and ecumenist, restricted by Rome in the 1950s, whose work on the laity, tradition and church reform shaped Vatican II’s documents on the Church, ecumenism and revelation. Made a cardinal in 1994.
people/john-milbank/summary: English Anglican theologian whose Theology and Social Theory (1990) argued that secular social science rests on disguised theological (often heretical) assumptions, and launched Radical Orthodoxy with Catherine Pickstock and Graham Ward (1999).
people/george-lindbeck/summary: Yale Lutheran theologian, born to missionary parents in China and a Lutheran observer at Vatican II, whose The Nature of Doctrine (1984) proposed a "cultural-linguistic" model in which doctrines function like grammatical rules of a community’s speech and life. With Hans Frei he founded postliberal theology.
people/stanley-hauerwas/summary: Texan theologian at Notre Dame and Duke, influenced by John Howard Yoder and Karl Barth, who argued that the Church’s first social ethic is to be a community of character and nonviolence rather than a chaplain to the nation. Time named him "America’s best theologian" in 2001.
people/james-cone/summary: African Methodist Episcopal minister and professor at Union Theological Seminary, New York, whose Black Theology and Black Power (1969) and A Black Theology of Liberation (1970) founded Black liberation theology, reading the gospel from the experience of Black Americans under white supremacy. His last major book, The Cross and the Lynching Tree (2011), set the cross beside lynching.
people/james-cone/keyIdeas/0: God is on the side of the oppressed
people/james-cone/keyIdeas/2: The cross and the lynching tree
